newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Dow's record 6,010 close buoys major Asian markets.
newsitem.headline: Dow's record 6,010 close buoys major Asian markets.

text.p: Wall Street's record overnight close pushed the Hong Kong and Australian bourses to record highs again on Tuesday and gave a boost to Tokyo.
But other Asian markets -- particularly Thailand's -- ignored the Dow's lead, falling on their own domestic political and economic problems.
The Dow Industrials ended up 40.99 to close at 6,010 on Monday, the first close ever above the key psychological 6000 level.

Tokyo stocks surged on the new Wall Street highs as well as speculation that the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) may win a majority in the Lower House of parliament in Japan's general election on Sunday, brokers said.
The benchmark Nikkei 225 jumped 400.68 points or 1.91 percent to close at 21,429.93.
"The Dow closed at over 6,000 and the domestic political picture is coming into focus with the LDP seen at the nucleus," said Yamaichi Securities general manager Tadahiro Kamogawa.

U.S. bullishness spilled over into Hong Kong, where the Hang Seng index recorded its third record closing high in less than a week. Driven higher by continued interest in property and banking stocks, the Hang Seng closed the session at a record 12,490.70, up 160.35 points or 1.30 percent.
"People are enjoying a bit of euphoria at the moment because U.S. interest rates did not go up," said Keith Irving, head of research at HG Asia. Four or five major stocks led the rally.

A Dow-inspired Australian share market ended at its second-straight record close. The key All Ordinaries index closed 2.9 points or 0.12 percent higher at 2,366.2, well off its intra-day and life-time high of 2,380.8.

The New Zealand share market rose 57.18 points or 2.53 percent to close at a new 32-month high of 2321.66 after weaker-than-expected CPI data prompted one of the largest rallies equities have seen this year, brokers said.

Brokers said the market had opened strongly, but the release of CPI data, which put core inflation at 2.4 percent in the September year against expectations of 2.7 percent, had caused a sharp fall in interest rates.
Domestic worries reigned in Thailand, where stocks fell for the fifth consecutive trading day on selling by foreigners worried about third quarter earnings and the economy.

After dipping below the 900-point mark, the SET index regained some ground to finish 12.96 points or 1.41 percent lower at 905.34. It was the lowest close since July 27, 1993, when the index finished at 893.14.
Seoul shares also tumbled, ending eight straight days of gains, but brokers shrugged off the losses and predicted the market would soon bounce back.
The composite stock index lost 13.67 points or 1.62 percent to close provisionally at 828.61.

Manila shares edged down as foreign funds continued to pocket gains to realign their portfolio in the region, traders said. The main index shaved off 8.43 points or 0.29 percent to close at 2,927.43 points.
Taiwan share prices ended slightly lower, down 10.03 points or 0.15 percent at 6,616.38.
Singapore's Straits Times Industrial Index closed up 14.90 points or 0.73 percent to 2,060.48 points while Malaysian equities ended up 7.55 points or 0.66 percent at 1156.40.
SIMEX Brent futures were slightly lower in late trade, attracting some profit taking after the overnight rally in London and New York futures.
November Brent futures were last traded at $24.80 per barrel, down six cents from London's overnight close of $24.86. December last traded down six at $24.32.

In Tokyo, the dollar rose but stalled under 112 yen on profit-taking sales which emerged as it approached that level. It rallied to 112.17 yen in Europe, its highest level since January 1994, after breaching the previous 1996 high at 112.10 from October 2, traders said.
At 1014 GMT, the dollar traded at 112.10/2.15 yen and 1.5362/65 marks.
Hong Kong's gold bullion opened at US$381.50/382.00, the day's high, and slowly slipped to close at US$381.00/381.50, the day's low.
